claims.detail: Between snapshots 2026-08-02 and 2026-09-02, 5.1% of tracked listings were delisted and 7.6% of survivors changed price.
limitations: Two snapshots one month apart cannot resolve intra-month price dynamics.
Delisting is measured only on fully paginated merchants, a minority of the corpus.
Catalog membership is a proxy for purchasable availability, not a checkout test.
claims.scope: Merchants that the later snapshot paginated in full, so that an absent SKU means a delisting rather than a page-cap truncation. One calibration and one evaluation date, one protocol, and no claim about retail commerce beyond this corpus.
claims.statement: Offers in the live UCP merchant corpus are ephemeral: between the two dated snapshots a measurable share of tracked listings is delisted and a measurable share of surviving listings changes price, so deciding when to stop searching is a real decision rather than a formality.

claims.detail: 5 enumerated instances checked; all agree with the solver in exact arithmetic.
limitations: Enumeration is only feasible for small horizons and small price supports.
Agreement on these instances does not by itself prove optimality in general.
Adaptive merchant routing is not covered by these fixed-order instances.
claims.scope: Registered instances with a fixed merchant order, discrete price supports, optional stockout weight, a hard purchase-price cap, and a terminal failure penalty, small enough for complete policy enumeration.
claims.statement: The finite-horizon stopping solver returns exactly the minimum expected purchase loss achievable by any deterministic accept-or-continue policy on every registered small instance, in exact rational arithmetic.

claims.detail: Paired mean difference -26.32 minor units over 152 held-out episodes; 95% CI upper bound -8.56 excludes zero.
limitations: The measured effect is statistically detectable but economically small, because most episodes in this corpus have near-identical prices across merchants.
Nearly every episode has exactly two merchants, so the result does not establish behaviour at longer search horizons.
Only two currencies survive the single-currency filter.
With two merchants the adaptive rule coincides with one-step lookahead, so this result does not separate the two policies.
claims.scope: Single-currency episodes in which one exact SKU is offered by at least two independent merchants, replayed under no-recall semantics with a per-episode failure penalty and a shared merchant arrival order.
claims.statement: On frozen held-out panels built from live UCP merchants, adaptive stopping attains lower failure-penalized purchase loss than the strongest fixed rule tuned on calibration data, with the whole paired bootstrap confidence interval below zero.

claims.detail: Adaptive stopping never wins at price dispersion at or below 1.01; 2 of 32 cells favour the fixed rule outright.
limitations: The generator is calibrated to the measured corpus but is still synthetic.
Prices are drawn independently across merchants; real merchants may co-move.
The reported thresholds are grid boundaries, not fitted decision surfaces, so the true boundary lies somewhere between adjacent grid levels.
claims.scope: A simulation sweep over merchant count, price dispersion, and budget fraction, with stockout and drift rates calibrated to the measured UCP corpus. Simulation evidence, not a live-panel measurement.
claims.statement: Adaptive stopping provides no measurable advantage over a tuned fixed rule when cross-merchant price dispersion is negligible, and can be significantly worse when the query budget is too tight to act on what a query reveals.

claims.detail: Closed form matches the solver to 0.02% across 8 horizons, and captures 81.5% of achievable savings against the solver's 89.8%.
limitations: The recursion and its asymptotic are established prior results (Cayley 1875; Moser 1956; Gilbert and Mosteller 1966; Finch 2024). No novelty is claimed for the formula itself.
The recursion carries no per-query cost term; cost enters only through the map from budget to remaining horizon.
Derived for a uniform price law; other shapes give a different acceptance fraction, though the two-step structure is unchanged.
Agreement is checked to a relative tolerance because the solver takes a discrete price support while the closed form is continuous.
Requires an estimate of the cheapest and dearest reachable price; a bad range estimate degrades the rule.
Savings capture is measured on the calibrated generator, not on live panels.
Reducing a multi-resource budget to a single query count is a modelling convention, not a result, and assumes deterministic per-query costs.
claims.scope: Prices uniform on a known range, a fixed per-query resource cost so the budget reduces to a count of affordable queries, and horizons up to eight further queries. The acceptance fraction follows u(0) = 1, u(k+1) = u(k) - u(k)^2 / 2, which under u = 1 - mu is the Cayley-Moser recursion mu(n) = (1 + mu(n-1)^2) / 2. This claim asserts correct reproduction of a known result, not a new one.
claims.statement: Our implementation reproduces the classical Cayley-Moser reservation sequence in a price-minimization parameterization: accepting when the observed price falls within a horizon-dependent fraction of the expected price range matches the exact solver to within grid-discretization error, and captures most of the savings the solver captures without running the dynamic program.

claims.detail: At 10 merchants the n/e rule captures 44.3% of achievable savings versus 81.5% for the closed-form threshold, costing 1936 more minor units while using 8.01 queries against 3.43.
limitations: That rank-based rules are suboptimal under a cardinal objective is established prior work (Bearden 2006; Palley and Kremer 2014). We measure the size of the penalty; we do not show the mismatch for the first time.
This compares the rules under an objective the secretary rule was never designed for; it is not a counterexample to the secretary result.
The comparison assumes a usable estimate of price levels. With no price knowledge at all, an ordinal rule is the appropriate tool.
Simulation evidence, not a live-panel measurement.
claims.scope: A calibrated simulation at a horizon long enough for exploration rules to differ, with stockout and drift rates taken from the measured corpus. The live corpus has too few merchants per episode to separate these rules.
claims.statement: We quantify a known information mismatch: the classical secretary rule, sampling n/e candidates before accepting the next record, captures substantially less of the achievable saving than a price threshold and spends more queries doing so, because it maximizes the chance of finding the single cheapest merchant rather than the expected price paid.

claims.detail: Across 2785 scanned merchants, 37750 products are offered by two or more independent sellers in a single currency, but only 4452 (11.8%) reach three or more. The widest observed overlap is 14 merchants.
limitations: Overlap is detected by exact SKU equality, so the same product listed under different identifiers at two merchants is counted as two products. The measured overlap is therefore a lower bound.
Merchants truncated at the pagination cap may carry additional shared products that were never observed.
One protocol on one date; not a claim about retail commerce generally.
claims.scope: Products offered by two or more independent registrable domains in a single currency, measured on the widest available discovery snapshot. Independence is by registrable domain, so multiple storefronts of one company count once.
claims.statement: Cross-merchant product overlap in the live UCP ecosystem is thin: after scanning every discoverable merchant, most products offered by more than one independent seller are offered by exactly two, and only a minority reach three or more. Since an optimal stopping rule and a one-step lookahead coincide when only one alternative remains, this bounds what any stopping policy can achieve here.

claims.detail: 0 hard-budget violations across every replayed episode and arm.
limitations: The evaluator confirms zero violations across the replayed episodes; it is evidence for the conjecture, not a proof of it.
The claim does not apply when an upstream service can spend beyond an issued permit.
claims.scope: Sequential merchant calls whose host runtime enforces each issued permit and whose reconciliation records cannot be forged, reused, or omitted.
claims.statement: Atomic reservation of every enforceable resource permit, followed by exact reclamation for known usage and permit-level charging for censored usage, keeps cumulative conservative charges within every initial episode budget on every execution path.

project.abstract: A shopping agent has to decide after each merchant: buy the offer in hand or pay to keep searching. A fixed threshold is easy to deploy, but it is unclear when a budget-aware decision can save enough to justify the time, calls, and spend of another search. We answer that question with live merchant data. Across two dated UCP catalog snapshots, listings disappear and surviving prices change within a month, while repeated scans minutes apart are byte-identical. We replay eight stopping policies on frozen held-out panels from those snapshots. An adaptive reservation-price rule lowers failure-penalized purchase loss relative to the strongest fixed rule tuned on calibration data; the paired bootstrap interval remains below zero, and every replay respects its hard budget. The improvement is statistically detectable but small because most matched products have only two merchants and little price variation. That limitation is the main finding, not a footnote: a calibrated sweep shows that adaptive stopping helps when merchants differ enough in price and the budget leaves room to use another observation. It is indistinguishable from a tuned fixed rule when prices are nearly identical and can be worse when the budget is too tight. We release the optimizer, replay harness, and collected panels.
project.subtitle: A measured decision rule for adaptive stopping under hard budgets
project.title: When Should a Shopping Agent Stop Searching?

decision_rule.interpretation: Continue only when the current offer is worse than the expected purchase loss from feasible future search.
